clue.text: Inspector General's interrupting electronic summons means death

indicators.note: the inspector's letters break into the middle of the summons word, interrupting it

parts.note: a bleep is the electronic signal that summons a doctor or engineer
IG is the abbreviation for Inspector General, with the S of the possessive

explanation.surface: A senior inspector's pager going off is a matter of life and death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'interrupting' puts IGS inside BLEEP. 'means' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Raymond Chandler's title phrase is a euphemism for the final rest of a corpse, so it stands for dying.

clue.text: Muslim ladies live on trees

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits on top of the second, so on signals order

parts.note: to be is to live or exist
gums are eucalyptus trees, also called gum trees

explanation.surface: Muslim women living up among the trees.
explanation.definitionFit: A begum is a Muslim woman of high rank in South Asia, a lady or princess.

clue.text: August, an arrangement for the other three lands

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'August, an arrangement for the other three lands', cannot give GUIANA: AUGUST AN has no I and an S and T the answer lacks; the fodder was probably IGUANA, but no scan or reprint confirms it.
annotationWithheld.clue: August, an arrangement for the other three lands

clue.text: Augustus' partner removed leaders from land

indicators.note: the leading letters of the land's name are taken away, the front pair dropped

parts.note: Bolivia is one of the South American lands that fill this grid

explanation.surface: The emperor's wife deposed the rulers of a country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'removed leaders from' drops BO from the front of BOLIVIA; 'leaders' is plural, so two letters go.
explanation.definitionFit: Livia Drusilla was the wife of the Roman emperor Augustus for over fifty years.

clue.text: Land with a hot line to Spain?

definitions.text: Land with a hot line to Spain?

parts.words: Land with a hot line to Spain?
parts.note: the hot line is the equator, which crosses this country, and its name is the Spanish word for that line, a link to Spain

explanation.surface: A country with a direct telephone link to Madrid.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'hot line' suggests a phone link, but here it is the line round the hottest part of the globe.
explanation.definitionFit: The South American republic takes its name from the Spanish word for the equator, which runs through it.

clue.text: Graduate having died, sailor gives monkey bread

parts.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate
ob, short for Latin obiit, means died
AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor

explanation.surface: After a graduate dies, a sailor hands out food for monkeys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gives' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Monkey bread is the common name for the African tree, and for its gourd-like fruit.

clue.text: A drink before the king's company goes to battle

indicators.note: in a down clue the drink comes first, before the company, setting the order

parts.note: gin is a drink
a court is the company of people around a monarch

explanation.surface: A tipple before the royal party sets off to fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes to' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry V defeated the French at this 1415 battle in northern France.

clue.text: Shop where they voice disapproval of hardwood?

indicators.note: to voice something is to say it, so the words are heard rather than read

parts.note: boo is a cry of disapproval; teak is a tropical hardwood

explanation.surface: A place where people jeer at a dense timber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'voice' does double duty in the surface (to voice disapproval) but signals that BOO TEAK is said to sound like the answer. 'where they' and 'of' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: A small fashionable store selling clothes or accessories is a type of retail outlet.

clue.text: Incidentally the Hebrew year is held in a space in the memory

indicators.note: the Hebrew and year letters are held inside the memory unit

parts.note: a byte is a unit of computer memory storage
Heb is the abbreviation for Hebrew

explanation.surface: By the way, a Jewish calendar year is stored in a computer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is held in' puts HEB and Y inside BYTE, after BYT. 'the' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom meaning by the way, said when mentioning a side remark.

clue.text: Lamentable and wayward giver has nothing for you and me

indicators.note: wayward means going off course, so the letters stray out of order

parts.note: O, a zero, is nothing
us means you and me

explanation.surface: A deplorable, unruly donor has nothing to give the two of us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wayward' rearranges GIVER into GRIEV. 'has' and 'for' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Something grievous is severe or causing great sorrow, so deplorable.

clue.text: Vexation that there's little time for a game of cards

parts.note: pique is irritation or vexation
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Annoyance that there is barely time for a hand of cards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little time' means a short form of time, T. 'that there's' and 'for' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: An old two-player card game played with a 32-card pack.

clue.text: Land of hope ruined

indicators.note: the land is made of letters from these two words, taken from inside them

explanation.surface: A country where all hope has been dashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' wants to be an anagram signal, but HOPE has no R or U; the answer runs across hoPE RUined.
explanation.definitionFit: Peru is a South American country, one of the lands in this grid.

clue.text: Give the push to a titled fellow?

parts.note: a fellow is a man
a handle is slang for a title, so a titled person has a handle

explanation.surface: Shove a nobleman aside.
explanation.walkthrough: A title is called a 'handle' (as in 'a handle to his name'), so a titled fellow is a man with a handle.
explanation.definitionFit: To manhandle someone is to push or move them roughly by force.

clue.text: Land where lowish temperatures are reported

indicators.note: a report is spoken, so the word is heard rather than written

parts.note: chilly describes fairly low temperatures

explanation.surface: A country where the weather forecast says it is cool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'where' is a link word; 'lowish temperatures' is an adjective phrase pointing to CHILLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Chile is the long narrow South American country, one of the lands in this grid.

clue.text: Tune on the piano for a duet

indicators.note: the tune is added on after the piano letter, giving the order

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical marking for soft
an air is a tune

explanation.surface: A melody played on the piano by two performers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A duet is performed by two people, a couple.

clue.text: Painting without data in a land

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside: the painting wraps round the data

parts.note: painting is a form of art
gen is British slang for information or data

explanation.surface: A picture lacking information in some country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside here, not lacking: ART goes round GEN. GEN is British slang for information.
explanation.definitionFit: Argentina is the large South American country, one of the lands in this grid.

clue.text: Always follow classy mentor back to the land

indicators.note: the word for always follows the earlier pieces, coming after them
back means the classy letter and the mentor word are read together from right to left

parts.note: U means upper class, as in U and non-U
a guru is a spiritual teacher or mentor
ay or aye is an old word for always

explanation.surface: Ever behind the stylish teacher heading home to his country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns U GURU into URUGU; 'follow' puts AY after. U for upper class is a British usage; AY (aye) is an old word for ever. 'to the' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Uruguay is a small South American country, one of the lands in this grid.

clue.text: Land of soft drink containing headless sleepwalker?

indicators.note: the drink word holds the other piece inside it

parts.note: cola is a fizzy soft drink

indicators.note: headless means losing the first letter

parts.note: a zombi or zombie walks about like someone asleep

explanation.surface: A country of fizzy pop with a decapitated walking dead inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'headless' takes Z off ZOMBI (a spelling of zombie) to give OMBI; 'containing' puts it inside COLA. 'of' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Colombia is the South American country on both Pacific and Caribbean coasts, one of the lands in this grid.

clue.text: Way in which D'Artagnan is largely still and stale

indicators.note: the way word has the other piece inside it

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way

indicators.note: largely means most of, so the musketeer's name loses its front letters

parts.note: D'Artagnan is the hero of Dumas's The Three Musketeers

explanation.surface: A road where the musketeer is mostly motionless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'largely' leaves TAGNAN, most of D'ARTAGNAN; 'in which' puts it inside ST. 'is' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Stagnant water does not flow and so goes foul, both motionless and stale.

clue.text: Figure a turncoat to go to the Pole

parts.note: read as two words, turn coat: the garment word with its letters turned about
taken as written
N, north, is a pole

explanation.surface: A traitor sets off for the Arctic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turncoat' looks like a traitor but splits into 'turn' and 'coat': COAT turned about gives OCTA. 'a' and 'to' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: An eight-sided polygon is a geometric shape.

clue.text: The boys in blue?

parts.note: the phrase usually means police officers, but here the sailors of the fleet, whose uniform is a dark blue

explanation.surface: A nickname for the police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The boys in blue' is a British nickname for the police; here it is the sea service, whose dark blue gives its name to a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A nation's sea force, its sailors in dark blue uniforms.

clue.text: Mewsical?

parts.note: a made-up word blending mew, the cry of a feline, with musical: a stage show full of mewing

explanation.surface: A one-word description of a show full of cries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mewsical' joins 'mew' to 'musical', pointing to Andrew Lloyd Webber's show based on T. S. Eliot's poems about felines.
explanation.definitionFit: The long-running Lloyd Webber stage show features felines that mew.

clue.text: Vocal piece, half a dance, "Goodbye"

indicators.note: half signals that only the first half of the dance word is used

parts.note: the cancan is a high-kicking dance
ta-ta is an informal goodbye

explanation.surface: A song cut halfway through a dance, then a farewell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' takes CAN from CANCAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A cantata is a choral or solo composition for voices with instruments.

clue.text: Sheridan the writer turned a leaf — new, one could say

indicators.note: turned means the letters are turned about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: spoken aloud, the word sounds like the two letters

parts.note: the word new, heard, gives two letters

explanation.surface: An author reformed, turning over a new leaf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' rearranges LEAF into LEFA; 'one could say' gives NU for the sound of NEW. 'a' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu was the Irish writer of ghost stories such as Carmilla.

clue.text: Gimcrack, T-Thomas the Tank Engine's author

parts.note: the stammered T before Thomas
the Rev. W. Awdry wrote the Railway Series stories of Thomas the Tank Engine

explanation.surface: A stammering reference to the creator of a children's train story.
explanation.walkthrough: The stammer 'T-Thomas' supplies an extra T in front of the author's surname, AWDRY.
explanation.definitionFit: Gimcrack describes showy but cheap goods, flashy and worthless.

clue.text: Music paper?

definitions.meaning: a keyboard instrument with pipes, played in churches
a newspaper or journal speaking for a party or group

explanation.surface: A two-word heading for sheet music.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a large pipe instrument and the periodical voice of an organization.

clue.text: Land that sounds like an Adriatic city craft with harpoons

indicators.note: the clue states plainly that the pieces are to be heard, not read

parts.words: an Adriatic city craft with harpoons
parts.note: Venice lies at the head of the Adriatic Sea; a whaler is a boat that hunts with harpoons

explanation.surface: A country named after a whaling ship from a lagoon city.
explanation.walkthrough: VENICE WHALER said quickly gives the answer; the country's name does mean 'little Venice'. 'that' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Venezuela is the northern South American country, one of the lands in this grid.

clue.text: Over here, beast!

definitions.meaning: a crossing point: where pedestrians go over the road
an African striped animal of the horse family

explanation.surface: A call to an animal to come across.
explanation.walkthrough: A zebra crossing is the British striped pedestrian crossing, a place to go over the road.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a striped wild horse and the British road crossing painted in its stripes.

clue.text: Nut land

definitions.meaning: a large three-sided nut from a South American tree

explanation.surface: A crazy country.
explanation.definitionFit: The country gives its name to a hard-shelled edible nut from its forests.

clue.text: The old Left put a home guard on the ship

parts.note: a lar is one of the Lares, Roman gods guarding the household
being on board is being on the ship

explanation.surface: Veteran left-wingers send a household guard on board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home guard' suggests Britain's wartime Home Guard volunteers; here it is a Roman household god. 'put' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: An old sailing word for the port side of a vessel, the side on your left facing forward.

clue.text: Off course like a carrier

parts.note: as means like
a tray is used to carry things

explanation.surface: A waiter drifting off route with a tray.
explanation.definitionFit: To go astray is to wander from the right path.

clue.text: Standard for a fellow without a land

parts.note: par is the standard or normal level

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside: the fellow goes round the letter

parts.note: a guy is a fellow

explanation.surface: A standard man lacking a country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside, not lacking: GUY goes round A. 'for' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Paraguay is a landlocked South American country, one of the lands in this grid.
